gloss_terse: To be complete, finished, spent; to consume, destroy; to accomplish or fulfill; to fail or languish
gloss_readable: A verb spanning the full arc from completion to exhaustion. In the Piel it means to finish a task or, more ominously, to consume and destroy utterly — often describing God's wrath devouring his enemies. In the Qal it portrays supplies running out, eyes failing from grief, or a period reaching its natural end. A specialized juridical sense appears when a matter is 'determined' as final. Across languages the translations split sharply: Arabic distinguishes akmala (complete) from afna (annihilate), and Korean separates 끝냈다 (finished a task) from 멸하다 (destroyed), confirming the genuine polysemy.

senses.1: The Piel transitive sense of bringing a defined work, speech, or activity to its intended conclusion. Arabic akmala and faragha, Korean 마쳤다/끝냈다, and Swahili -maliza all center on purposeful task completion. Prominent in narratives of building (Gen 6:16, the ark) and covenant speech (Gen 17:22, God finishing speaking with Abraham).
senses.2: The Piel sense of utter annihilation — consuming people or nations in divine wrath. Arabic afna/yufni, Korean 멸하다, and Swahili -angamiza point to destruction rather than mere completion. Central to Exodus 32:10-12 where God threatens to consume Israel after the golden calf, and to prophetic oracles of judgment.
senses.3: The Qal intransitive sense of reaching a natural end: supplies depleting, a period expiring, or a process ceasing. Arabic nafida (be exhausted) and Korean 없어지다 (disappear) capture the depletion nuance. Seen in Gen 21:15 where the water in Hagar's skin runs out, and 1 Kgs 17:14 where the widow's flour shall not come to an end.
senses.4: A Qal sense of failing, languishing, or becoming faint — especially of the eyes, soul, or strength giving way under grief or longing. Arabic kallat (eyes failed) and Korean 쇠하다 (weaken) mark exhaustion of the person rather than a supply. Concentrated in the Psalms (31:10, 69:3) and Job (11:20, 19:27), expressing deep emotional or physical depletion.
senses.5: The Piel sense of spending or expending resources — arrows, days, or provisions — where the emphasis is on depletion of a supply rather than destruction of persons. Arabic atimmu (I expended) and Korean 소모하다 (consume resources) fit precisely. Ps 90:9 says we spend our years like a sigh; Isa 49:4 laments strength spent in vain.
senses.6: A specialized Qal sense meaning 'be determined' or 'be decreed,' where completion shades into the finality of a judicial or divine decision. Arabic qudiyat (it was decreed), Korean 결정되었다 (was decided), and Swahili -amuliwa (was judged) all confirm the legal register. Key in 1 Sam 20:7, 9 where Jonathan discerns that harm is 'determined' by Saul against David.
senses.7: The Qal sense of fulfilling or accomplishing a divine purpose or prophetic plan. Arabic itmam (fulfillment) and Korean 성취하다 (achieve) point to teleological completion. Seen in 1 Kgs 6:38 — Solomon's temple was 'finished' in accord with its design — and 2 Chr 36:22 / Ezra 1:1 where the LORD's word through Jeremiah is 'accomplished.'
senses.8: The Pual passive: to be brought to completion by an external agent, the work finished upon the subject. Arabic uktumilat (was completed) and Korean 완성되었다 (was completed) both encode passivity. Gen 2:1 — the heavens and earth 'were finished' — provides the paradigmatic instance; Ps 72:20 marks the prayers of David as 'ended.'
senses.9: A single occurrence in 2 Sam 13:39 where David's spirit 'longed' or 'was consumed' with desire to go out to Absalom. The multilingual glosses (English 'she-longed,' Spanish 'y-ceso') suggest an emotional consuming or yearning — the verb's completion semantics turned inward as psychological exhaustion of desire.
senses.10: A single occurrence in Isa 27:10 describing desolation: the fortified city is consumed or laid waste. Spanish y-consumira and German und-Vernichtung (and-annihilation) align this with the destructive Piel sense applied to a place rather than persons.
senses.11: A single occurrence in Dan 11:16 where the invader shall stand in the glorious land 'with destruction in his hand.' English 'and-destruction' and the domain of VIOLENCE/CONFLICT mark this as a nominal or infinitival use denoting utter devastation as a military outcome.

gloss_terse: To be high or exalted; to lift up, raise; to extol or praise; to contribute an offering; to remove
gloss_readable: One of the great vertical-axis verbs of Hebrew, spanning physical lifting, social exaltation, and liturgical offering. In the Qal it describes something that is high, tall, or exalted — whether a person's stature, God's transcendence, or a heart swelling with pride. The Hifil adds causative force: raising a hand in oath (Gen 14:22), lifting up the poor, or presenting a heave offering. The Piel intensifies into praise and worship. Arabic rafa'a and Swahili -inua both mirror this physical-to-figurative trajectory, while Korean distinguishes 높은 (stative height) from 높이다 (active exaltation), tracking the Qal/Hifil split precisely.

senses.1: The Hifil causative sense of physically lifting, raising, or picking up a concrete object or person. Arabic rafa'a (to raise), Korean 들어올리다 (lift up), and Swahili -inua all converge on bodily, upward motion. Gen 14:22 (Abraham raises his hand to the LORD) and Gen 31:45 (Jacob lifts a stone) are paradigmatic examples of literal elevation.
senses.2: The Qal intransitive sense of rising, becoming exalted, or being lifted in status or glory. Arabic yartafi'u (to rise up), Korean 높아지다 (become high), and Swahili -inuliwa mark a change of state rather than an action. Key in Deut 8:14 where the heart 'is lifted up' in prosperity, and Num 24:7 where Israel's kingdom shall 'be exalted.'
senses.3: The Piel intensive sense of actively praising, extolling, or exalting — making someone's name great through worship or acclaim. Arabic 'azzama (magnify) and Korean 높이다 (intensive exalt) reflect deliberate, repeated praise. Exod 15:2 ('I will exalt him') and Ps 99:5 ('Exalt the LORD our God') exemplify this doxological register.
senses.4: A Qal stative or participial sense describing physical height, tallness of persons or objects, or a voice being loud. Arabic murtafi' (elevated), Korean 높은 (high/tall), and Swahili -refu (tall) all mark an enduring quality rather than an event. Deut 1:28 ('cities great and tall') and Num 33:3 ('with a high hand') illustrate this descriptive use.
senses.5: The Hifil causative sense of exalting a person in rank, honor, or power — making someone great in social standing. Arabic rafa'a (figurative), Korean 높이다 (elevate in status), and Swahili -inua (figurative promotion) all extend physical lifting to social elevation. Key in 1 Sam 2:10 where the LORD exalts the horn of his anointed.
senses.6: The Hifil sense of lifting up a ritual heave offering (terumah) or voluntary contribution to the sanctuary. Arabic qaddama (present/offer), Korean 바치다 (dedicate/offer), and Swahili -toa (give/present) all reflect a specialized cultic register. Exod 35:24 and Num 31:28, 52 show Israel presenting contributions for the tabernacle and war spoils.
senses.7: A Qal participial or stative sense applied to God's transcendent majesty — the Exalted One who dwells on high. Arabic muta'alin (the Most High) and Korean 높으시도다 (how exalted!) both reserve distinct doxological vocabulary for this sense. Ps 113:4 ('The LORD is high above all nations') and Ps 46:10 ('I will be exalted') are central texts.
senses.8: The Hifil sense of removing or taking away by lifting something off or clearing it from the path. Arabic azala (remove) and Korean 제거하다 (eliminate) shift the vertical metaphor to separation. Isa 57:14 ('take up the stumbling block') and Ezek 21:26 ('remove the turban') illustrate lifting-as-removal in prophetic speech.
senses.9: A Qal participial sense with negative moral connotation: haughty, arrogant, lifted up in pride. Arabic al-mutakabbirina (the arrogant ones), Korean 교만한 (proud), and Swahili -enye kiburi (having arrogance) all mark moral censure. Prov 6:17 ('haughty eyes') and Isa 2:12 (the LORD's day against all that is 'lifted up') warn against self-exaltation.
senses.10: The Hitpael reflexive sense of exalting oneself or magnifying oneself, typically with negative connotations. Arabic yartafi'u (reflexive rise) and Korean 높이리라 (self-exaltation) capture the self-directed action. Isa 33:10 ('Now I will arise, now I will be exalted') and Dan 11:36 where the king 'shall exalt himself' above every god show both divine and impious uses.
senses.11: The Pual or Hofal passive sense of being raised or exalted by another agent. Arabic rufi'a (was raised), Korean 높여진 (having been exalted), and Swahili -inuliwa (was lifted) encode patient-role promotion. Neh 9:5 ('blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted') and Ps 75:10 ('the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up') illustrate divine or communal honoring.

gloss_terse: To whirl, writhe, dance; to travail in labor; to tremble in fear; to bring forth, be born; to wait
gloss_readable: A remarkably physical verb whose root evokes circular, convulsive motion. It covers writhing in anguish, trembling before God's majesty, the contractions of childbirth, joyful dancing, and even patient waiting. Arabic decisively separates these senses with entirely different roots — tawajja'a for pain, irtaʿada for trembling, tamakhkhada for labor, raqasa for dancing, and intazara for waiting — confirming that these are genuinely distinct meanings rather than translation artifacts. The spectrum from agony to celebration makes this one of Hebrew's most evocative verbs.

senses.1: The Qal sense of writhing in pain or anguish, conveying intense physical or emotional suffering. Arabic tawajja'a (Form V, specifically 'suffer pain') uses a root distinct from trembling or labor, confirming a standalone pain sense. Isa 13:8 ('they will be in anguish like a woman in labor') and Ps 55:4 ('my heart writhes within me') are central passages.
senses.2: The Qal sense of trembling or quaking in fear, particularly before God's awe-inspiring presence. Arabic irtaʿada (Form VIII of r-ʿ-d, 'tremble/quake'), from a completely different root than pain or labor, marks genuine semantic independence. Ps 29:8 ('the LORD shakes the wilderness') and 1 Chr 16:30 ('tremble before him, all the earth') show the theophanic setting.
senses.3: The Piel causative-intensive sense of bringing forth or causing to bear — begetting life. Arabic walada (give birth) and anjaba (Form IV, 'cause to beget') use birthing-specific roots distinct from pain, trembling, or whirling. Deut 32:18 ('the Rock that begot you') and Ps 90:2 ('before the mountains were brought forth') exemplify divine and cosmic generation.
senses.4: The Qal sense of travailing or being in labor during childbirth. Arabic tamakhkhada (Form V of m-kh-d, exclusively 'parturition') provides a root with no overlap with general pain or trembling. Isa 54:1 ('sing, O barren one, who did not travail') and Job 39:1 ('do you know when the mountain goats give birth?') anchor this obstetric sense.
senses.5: The Pual or Hofal passive of the birthing sense: to be brought forth, to be born, to be formed. Arabic wulida (passive of walada) and takawwana ('be formed') encode patient-role creation. Prov 8:24-25 ('before the depths I was brought forth') and Ps 51:5 ('in sin my mother conceived me') express origins through this passive voice.
senses.6: The Qal sense of whirling or swirling — circular, spiraling motion. Arabic dalla/yahullu ('descend/alight') and dara ('go round') use rotation vocabulary unrelated to pain or birthing, while Korean 소용돌이치다 (whirl/eddy) matches precisely. Jer 23:19 ('a whirling tempest') and Hos 11:6 ('the sword shall whirl in their cities') show destructive rotary force.
senses.7: The Qal or Hitpael sense of waiting or tarrying patiently. Arabic intazara (Form VIII of n-z-r, 'look/wait') has zero overlap with pain, trembling, or birthing roots, confirming a distinct semantic field. Gen 8:10 (Noah 'waited' another seven days) and Ps 37:7 ('wait patiently for the LORD') ground this sense in narrative and wisdom literature.
senses.8: The Qal sense of dancing in joyful celebration. Arabic raqasa ('to dance'), a root entirely distinct from all other senses of this verb, and Korean 춤추다 ('to dance'), a dedicated dance lexeme, both confirm the standalone meaning. Judg 21:21, 23 — the daughters of Shiloh dancing at the annual feast — provides the sole but vivid attestation.
senses.9: The Qal sense of being wounded or pierced, attested in battle narrative. Arabic juriha (passive of jarraha 'wound'), from the root j-r-h exclusively meaning physical wounding, separates this from general pain. 1 Sam 31:3 and its parallel 1 Chr 10:3 describe Saul being 'wounded' by Philistine archers — a martial context.
senses.10: A single occurrence in Lam 4:6 where the English gloss 'rested' and Spanish 'se-pusieron' suggest something settled or came to rest. In context, the verse compares Zion's punishment to Sodom's overthrow, possibly indicating that suffering 'came upon' or 'fell upon' the city — an extension of the convulsive-motion root toward sudden descent.
senses.11: A single occurrence in Jer 4:19, marked as a ketiv reading, where the prophet cries out in anguish. The Spanish gloss 'me-duelo' (I grieve) and the emotional context suggest an internal writhing or heart-pounding that overlaps with sense 1 (writhing in pain), though the textual variant makes the reading uncertain.

gloss_terse: To pass over, through, or by; to cross a boundary; to transgress; to remove; to proclaim; to overflow
gloss_readable: The fundamental Hebrew verb of transit and crossing. At its core it describes movement from one side to the other — whether fording the Jordan, passing through a land, or traversing a road. From this spatial root grow powerful figurative extensions: crossing a moral boundary becomes transgression, causing a proclamation to 'pass through' a camp becomes public announcement, and causing something to 'pass over' from one owner to another becomes legal transfer. Arabic 'abara preserves this same physical-to-abstract trajectory. The word gives its name to the 'Hebrews' themselves (ivrim, 'those who crossed over'), binding Israel's identity to the act of boundary-crossing.

senses.1: The Qal sense of passing by, passing through, or passing along without emphasis on crossing a specific boundary — general transit through a region or along a route. Arabic 'abara (pass) and Korean 지나가다 (pass by) capture the unmarked movement sense. Gen 12:6 (Abram 'passed through' the land to Shechem) and Josh 15:3-4 (border descriptions) are paradigmatic.
senses.2: The Qal sense of crossing over a definitive physical boundary — a river, sea, or border. Arabic 'abara (cross) and Korean 건너다 (cross over) both specify boundary-traversal. This is the great exodus verb: Israel crossing the Jordan (Josh 3-4), Jacob crossing the Jabbok (Gen 32:22), and the programmatic formula 'when you cross over into the land' (Deut passim).
senses.3: The Qal sense of passing away, ceasing, or vanishing — temporal passing of time, seasons, grief, or life itself. Arabic intaha (come to an end) and Korean 지나가다 (pass, elapse) extend spatial transit to temporal cessation. 2 Sam 11:27 ('when the mourning had passed') and 1 Kgs 18:29 ('midday passed') show duration reaching its limit.
senses.4: The Hifil causative sense of bringing across or causing to cross a physical boundary — leading people over a river, ferrying goods, or dedicating firstborn by 'causing them to pass through.' Gen 32:23 (Jacob sends his family across the ford) and Exod 13:12 ('you shall cause to pass over to the LORD every firstborn') illustrate both literal and ritual crossing.
senses.5: The Qal sense of transgressing or violating a covenant, commandment, or moral boundary. Arabic ta'adda (overstep) and Korean 범하다 (violate) map the physical crossing metaphor onto ethical breach. Deut 17:2 ('transgressing his covenant'), 1 Sam 15:24 ('I have transgressed the LORD's command'), and Josh 7:11 ('Israel has transgressed my covenant') are central texts.
senses.6: The Hifil sense of removing or taking away — causing something to pass from its place. Arabic azala (remove) and Korean 제거하다 (eliminate) reframe crossing as displacement. 2 Sam 12:13 ('the LORD has put away your sin') and 2 Sam 24:10 ('take away the iniquity of your servant') show removal of guilt, while Gen 47:21 describes removing populations to cities.
senses.7: The Hifil sense of causing a voice, decree, or trumpet blast to 'pass through' a camp or land — issuing a proclamation. Arabic a'lana (announce publicly) and Korean 선포하다 (proclaim) encode the broadcast metaphor. Exod 36:6 ('Moses commanded and they caused it to pass through the camp') and 2 Chr 30:5 ('they sent proclamation throughout all Israel') illustrate the idiom.
senses.8: The Hifil sense of transferring or conveying ownership, possession, or inheritance from one party to another. Arabic naqala (transfer) and Korean 넘기다 (hand over) specify legal conveyance. Num 27:7-8 ('you shall cause the inheritance to pass over to them') and Esth 8:2 (the king's signet ring transferred to Mordecai) reflect property and authority transfer.
senses.9: The Qal sense of overflowing or surging — water or liquid rising beyond its banks or streaming abundantly. Arabic fada (overflow) and Korean 흘러넘치다 (overflow) apply the transit metaphor to liquids exceeding boundaries. Song 5:5, 13 ('myrrh flowing/passing') and Isa 23:10 ('pass through your land like the Nile') evoke abundance and flooding.
senses.10: The Piel intensive sense of impregnating or breeding — causing to pass through in a reproductive context. Arabic laqaha (breed/impregnate) and Korean 교배시키다 (cause to breed) confirm the specialized biological register. Job 21:10 ('his bull breeds and does not fail') provides the clearest attestation, while 1 Kgs 6:21 may involve drawing chains across the inner sanctuary.
